description: We are mapping for the future! Our team joins skills from computer engineering, bioinformatics, and computer science. Our skills expand fields of computer science, physics, Math, Biology, Chemistry, Statistics, ML, AI, Software Engineering, and web development. We are STEM enthusiasts and eager to learn and explore!!
summary:
Marswalk helps astronauts plan and carry out walks on Mars using real NASA data.
The landing page is a six-scene 3D scroll story. It goes from Mars orbit down to Jezero crater and Perseverance on its real track. The rover then comes apart into 65 named parts, which reassemble into NASA’s Z-2 suit, ending with a view through the visor. It works on phones and has a reduced-motion version.
Plan a walk opens on a Mars globe with ten sites and ice layers. The Jezero planner works out routes over real terrain, compares three of them, and keeps away from sand ridges. Walking maps cover nine more sites, plus a weather outlook from Curiosity’s records and a check of whether each site is workable.
Identify the ground runs a terrain model in the browser. It labels a photo as soil, bedrock, sand or big rock and gives plain-language hazard cards.
Mars in 3D shows terrain with routing, a simulated walk, and a probe that reads elevation and slope.
Helmet view turns a phone camera into a visor with live ground colours.
The habitat and suit tag hardware uses radio beacons for live position, telemetry, hazard and fall alerts, and buddy tracking. It has been tested at a real Earth site.
The terrain model was trained on NASA’s AI4Mars rover photos.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Marswalk is a browser-based planning tool for astronaut walks (EVAs) on Mars. It opens on a spinning globe of Mars built from NASA’s Viking colour mosaic. Pick one of ten sites and the map zooms into a walking map: Jezero, Gale, Gusev, Meridiani, Utopia, the Phoenix landing site, Arcadia, and one tile each at Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris and Hellas.

Each walking map is a 30 m grid built from real orbital terrain models, mostly 1 m HiRISE stereo models. The astronaut places a habitat and clicks targets. The planner then:

• routes over the terrain with A*, refusing slopes steeper than an adjustable limit;.

• compares three candidate routes (shortest, terrain-aware, recommended) and explains in metres why each differs;.

• checks every route against a 30-minute walk-back rule from NASA JSC’s 2026 suit study, the daylight window and a radiation dose budget;.

• gives three return options from the farthest point (primary, alternate, emergency);.

• on canyon and volcano sites, computes where the crew can still walk back to the habitat, where terrain blocks radio line of sight to it, and a feasibility verdict for the planned route..

The same routes run in a 3D view, where an astronaut avatar walks the route over real slopes. At rover sites, the rover’s real drives count as proven ground, and its measurements (weather, radiation, rock chemistry, its own tilt) are pinned where they were taken. A weather outlook projects conditions from Curiosity’s measured weather history. A phone “helmet view” and a photo tool that identifies the ground type complete it.

What benefits does it have?

• Honest by design. Every value is labelled as measured, mapped from orbit, calculated, a draft assumption, or simulated. Missing data shows as “not characterized”, never as fine. The tool never calls ground “safe”..

• Real data, cited. Every layer shows its source, resolution and date..

• Comparable sites. A side-by-side table lists the same facts for every site: elevation, calculated air pressure, and what was actually measured on the surface. It uses facts instead of invented scores..

• Plain language. Technical terms carry hover explanations, so people with no space background can follow..

• Adjustable rules. Walk speed, walk-back limit and slope limit are sliders. Every check updates when they change, so the tool stays useful once suit engineers publish real limits..

What is the intended impact of the project?

To help mission planners, students and the public see what walking on Mars would actually take. That means the terrain, the distances, the time, and how far the crew can go and still get back. It also shows clearly how much of what we “know” about each site was measured on the ground, and how much is inferred from orbit or simply unknown. The goal is better questions about future landing sites and suit design, not false confidence.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

• Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the app; Python for the data pipeline..

• App libraries: Leaflet for the 2D map, three.js for 3D terrain and the avatar, ONNX Runtime Web for the photo classifier..

• Data processing: Python with NumPy, SciPy, Pillow and tifffile. It reads only the needed bytes from NASA archives using HTTP range requests..

• Data sources:.

◦ NASA Mars Trek map tiles;.

◦ HiRISE stereo terrain models from the HiRISE PDS archive;.

◦ MGS MOLA elevation and Mars Express HRSC images from the PDS Geosciences Node;.

◦ Odyssey THEMIS infrared;.

◦ the Perseverance and Curiosity traverses from NASA MMGIS, and the corrected Spirit and Opportunity traverses from the PDS Geosciences Node;.

◦ Curiosity REMS weather and RAD radiation results;.

◦ the SWIM ice maps, SHARAD results and published papers..

• Testing and tooling: headless Microsoft Edge driven over the Chrome DevTools Protocol with Node.js, Git and GitHub, and Vercel for hosting..

• Hardware: a laptop. The app is designed for an ESP32 suit tag sending position and vitals over LoRa, but that link is not built yet; crew position is simulated and labelled so..

How is your project creative?

• It plans walks, not drives. It turns orbital datasets made for rovers and science into a footstep-scale walk planner with human rules: walk-back time, slope and dose..

• It shows confinement as a map. In Valles Marineris and on the Olympus Mons escarpment it maps where a crew can still get home and where canyon walls block line of sight to the habitat antenna. The danger becomes visible rather than reduced to a rating..

• It ties rovers to the walk. Real rover tracks double as proven ground and as ground truth for the terrain models..

• It is honest about uncertainty. The tool explains its own uncertainty instead of hiding it behind scores..

• It is a whole package. A spinning globe, 3D walking avatar, phone helmet view and photo identifier make the data approachable for non-experts..

What factors did your team consider?

• Scientific accuracy: every number traced to a source. Claims we couldn’t verify were left out, and positions were checked against the terrain. For example, we fitted Opportunity’s track to Victoria crater’s rim because it was about 140 m off..

• Human limits: NASA JSC’s 2026 walk-back rule, an illustrative slope limit until suit data exists, daylight, and radiation at the Curiosity-measured rate..

• Data limits: terrain model resolution, coverage gaps, stereo errors, and the difference between a landform seen from orbit and a measurement..

• Safety language: no “safe” labels, no hazard rings or volcanic risk ratings without evidence, and missing data shown as not characterized..

• Accessibility: plain-language explanations, a phone-friendly layout, and clear labels for everything simulated..

• Performance: routing and the walk-back maps compute in the browser in well under a second, with terrain files of a few megabytes.
